title: Spread Plate Method

references.label: Biosafety in Microbiological and Biomedical Laboratories (BMBL)

purpose: To evenly distribute a measured volume of diluted sample across an agar surface, producing separated colonies suitable for isolation or for viable colony counting (CFU enumeration).
principle: A small, accurately measured volume of a diluted suspension is deposited on the agar surface and spread thinly and evenly with a sterile spreader, so that most viable cells land far enough apart to each form a single, countable colony.
requiredMaterials: Sterile L-shaped spreader (or bent glass rod) or a sterile disposable spreader
requiredReagents: 70% ethanol (for flame-sterilizing a reusable spreader, if used)

procedure.instruction: Label the plate base with sample ID, dilution, date, and initials.

Pipette a small, precisely measured volume of the diluted sample (commonly on the order of 0.1 mL, but the exact volume must be recorded since it is a direct term in the CFU/mL formula) onto the center of the agar surface.
Sterilize the spreader (e.g. dip in ethanol and flame briefly, letting the flame extinguish before touching the plate) if using a reusable spreader; allow it to cool.
Spread the liquid evenly across the entire agar surface, rotating the plate as needed, without gouging the agar.
Allow the plate to sit undisturbed for several minutes so the liquid absorbs into the agar.
Incubate inverted at the appropriate temperature/duration for the organism.

observations: Well-spread plates show individual, separated colonies distributed across the surface rather than concentrated in one area.
interpretation: Colony count on a spread plate, combined with the known volume plated and dilution factor, is used directly in the CFU/mL calculation (see the CFU/mL Calculator).
precautions: Ensure the spreader has cooled after flaming before it touches the agar or the culture — a hot spreader kills cells.
Record the exact volume plated; guessing this value invalidates any CFU calculation from the plate.
limitations: Plates with too many or too few colonies fall outside the countable range for the method being followed and should not be used for enumeration (see the CFU/mL Calculator's countability note).
biosafetyNotes: Containment requirements depend on the organism being enumerated, not on the spread plate method itself.
